30 mph zone: A road area where the speed limit is 30 miles per hour, common in built-up areas in the UK.
ABS brakes: Anti-lock braking system that helps you steer while braking hard in an emergency.
ABS: Anti-lock braking system that helps you steer while braking hard in an emergency.
AED: Automated external defibrillator: a device that can shock the heart back to rhythm.
Advisory speed: A recommended speed for safety that is not a legal maximum limit.
Aerial: The radio antenna on a vehicle, often a thin rod on the roof or rear.
Anti-lock brakes: ABS: brakes that help stop the wheels locking under hard braking.
Anticipate traffic ahead: Look far ahead and prepare early for what other vehicles will do.
Antifreeze: A liquid mixed with water in the cooling system to stop it freezing in cold weather.
Average speed check zone: A stretch where cameras measure your average speed between two points.
Average speed zone: An area where cameras check your average speed over a stretch of road.
Blue Badge: A UK disability parking badge that gives certain parking concessions.
Boot: The storage compartment at the back of a car (called the trunk in some countries).
Brake fluid: Hydraulic fluid that transfers pressure from the brake pedal to the brakes.
Brake sharply: Press the brake hard so the vehicle slows or stops suddenly.
Breakdown cover: A service that helps if your vehicle stops working on the road.
Breakdown recovery: A vehicle that helps remove or repair broken-down vehicles on the road.
Bumper: The protective bar at the front or rear of a vehicle designed to absorb minor impacts.
Bus lane: A lane reserved mainly for buses (and sometimes taxis or cycles) at certain times.
CPR: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation: chest compressions (and breaths) to help someone not breathing.
Chassis number: The unique identification number stamped on the vehicle's frame.
Clutch: The pedal/system that disconnects the engine from the wheels when changing gear.
Coast in neutral: Rolling without a gear engaged, so the engine does not help slow the vehicle.
Coast: To roll without engine drive (e.g. in neutral), which reduces control.
Collapsible steering wheel: A steering column designed to fold in a crash to reduce injury.
Comprehensive: A wide motor insurance level that can cover your own vehicle as well as damage to others.
Congestion charges: Fees charged to drive into certain busy city zones to reduce traffic.
Contraflow systems: A temporary traffic system where vehicles travel in the opposite direction to normal, often during roadworks.
Corner steadies: Support legs at the corners of a caravan used to keep it stable when parked, not while towing.
Crossroads: A junction where two roads cross each other.
Cycle lane: A part of the road reserved for cyclists, often marked with a bicycle symbol.
Cycle route: A path or lane intended for bicycles.
Dazzles: Temporarily blinds other drivers with bright light so they cannot see clearly.
Dazzling: Blinding other drivers with bright lights so they cannot see properly.
Defensive: A careful driving style that anticipates hazards and leaves a safety margin.
Dipped headlights: Headlights aimed lower so they light the road without dazzling oncoming drivers.
Double bend ahead: A warning that two bends follow closely, one after the other.
Double white lines: Two white lines along the centre of the road that restrict crossing and parking.
Driving licence: The official card that shows you are allowed to drive certain vehicles.
Dual carriageway: A major road with traffic travelling in opposite directions, separated by a central reservation.
ESC: Electronic Stability Control: a system that helps keep the car stable if wheels start to lose grip.
Edge forward: Move the vehicle slowly ahead a short distance.
End of restrictions: A sign meaning earlier parking or waiting limits no longer apply beyond that point.
Etching registration: Permanently marking the vehicle’s number plate onto glass or parts.
Exhaust system: The pipes and parts that carry waste gases from the engine out of the vehicle.
Extended-arm side mirrors: Door mirrors on longer arms so you can still see past a wide trailer or caravan.
Exterior towing mirrors: Extra or extended side mirrors required when a trailer is wider than the towing vehicle.
First-aiders: People trained to give basic emergency care before professionals arrive.
Flash headlights: Briefly switch the headlights on and off to get someone's attention.
Flash your headlights: Briefly switching headlights on and off to attract attention; not a reliable way to give instructions.
Flushed skin: Skin that looks unusually red or warm, for example from heat or emotion.
Front fog lights: Extra front lights used only when visibility is seriously reduced, such as in thick fog.
Full beam: Headlights aimed high for maximum range; can dazzle oncoming drivers.
GPS: A sat-nav system that gives turn-by-turn directions while you drive.
Gearbox: The part of the car that contains the gears for changing speed and power.
Give way: Let other traffic go first when they have priority, instead of continuing ahead of them.
Handbrake: The parking brake that holds the vehicle still when stopped.
Handling: How the car steers, corners, and responds; a heavy load can make this worse.
Hazard lights: All indicators flashing together to warn others of danger or a problem.
Hazardous materials: Dangerous substances such as chemicals or fuel that need special care in transport.
Heavy goods vehicles: Large trucks that carry freight; often called HGVs in the UK.
High gear: A higher gear used for faster cruising, with less engine braking effect than a low gear.
High-sided vehicles: Tall vehicles such as lorries or vans that can be pushed sideways by strong wind.
Highway Code: The official UK rules and advice for road users.
Hill starts: Moving off from a standstill on an uphill slope without rolling back.
Jockey wheel: A small wheel near the trailer hitch used to support and manoeuvre the trailer when unhitched.
Junction on a bend: A side road joining the main road on a curve, which can reduce visibility.
Kerbs: The raised stone or concrete edge between the road and the pavement.
Lap belt: A seat belt that goes only across the hips, without a diagonal shoulder strap.
Licensing authority: The official body that issues and manages driving licences and related vehicle records (e.g. DVLA).
Local authority recycling site: A council tip or recycling centre that accepts items like used engine oil.
Local diversion route: A temporary alternative path around a closed or blocked road.
Loose gravel: Small loose stones on the road surface that can reduce tyre grip.
Lorry: A large goods truck used to carry heavy loads (UK term for a truck).
Low gear: A lower gear ratio that gives more engine control at slower speeds, often used on hills.
MOT certificate: A UK document showing a vehicle has passed its annual roadworthiness test.
MOT expiry date: The date when the current MOT certificate runs out and a new test is needed.
MOT test: The UK annual check that a vehicle is safe and roadworthy.
MOT: The annual UK roadworthiness test required for most vehicles over a certain age.
MOTs: UK annual roadworthiness tests (MOT) checking safety and emissions.
Main beam headlights: Full high-beam headlights that light farther ahead but can dazzle other drivers.
Main beam: High-beam headlights that light farther ahead but can dazzle other road users.
Mandatory instruction: An order you must follow, not just advice.
Mandatory rules: Rules you are legally required to obey.
Manufacturer's handbook: The official owner’s manual from the car maker explaining controls and systems.
National Insurance number: A UK personal tax and benefits reference number, not a driving document.
No loading: A restriction meaning goods must not be loaded or unloaded there at the times shown.
No parking: You must not leave the vehicle parked, but brief stopping to drop off may be allowed.
No stopping: A ban on stopping your vehicle at all, even briefly (stricter than no parking).
No waiting: A UK restriction meaning you must not wait or park there at the times shown.
Oil seals: Rubber or metal rings that stop oil leaking from the engine.
Oncoming headlights: The headlights of vehicles coming toward you from the opposite direction.
One-way road: A road where traffic is allowed to travel in only one direction.
Over-rev: Run the engine at very high revs, which wastes fuel and can cause wear.
Overtake: To pass another vehicle by moving past it and going ahead.
Overtaking vehicles: Vehicles that are passing you on the road.
Overtaking: Passing a slower vehicle ahead by moving into another lane or the other side of the road.
P plates: Optional plates some newly qualified drivers display to show they have just passed their test.
Paramedics: Emergency medical staff who treat patients at the scene and in ambulances.
Parking/sidelights: Low-intensity lights used to show a parked or stationary vehicle’s position.
Powered mobility vehicles: Small electric vehicles used by people with limited mobility.
Primary route: A main A-road network in the UK, usually signed with green direction signs.
Projection markers: Flags or lights that mark an overhanging load so other road users can see it.
Pull alongside: Drive level with another vehicle, side by side.
Rear fog lights: Bright red lights at the back of a vehicle used only in thick fog to help others see you.
Registered keeper: The person named on the vehicle’s registration document as responsible for it (not always the owner).
Restricted airspace: Air above an area where flying is limited or controlled for safety.
Rev engine: Make the engine run faster while the vehicle is not moving forward much.
Ride the clutch: Holding the clutch partly down while driving, which can wear it and reduce control.
Road gritter: A vehicle that spreads salt or grit on roads to reduce ice in cold weather.
Road narrows: A warning that the carriageway becomes narrower ahead.
Road sweeper: A slow vehicle that cleans the road surface; give it space when passing.
Road tax: Vehicle Excise Duty — the UK government charge for using a vehicle on public roads.
Road works: Construction or repairs on the road that may change lanes or reduce speed.
Roadworks: Road repairs or construction that may change layout, lanes, or speed limits.
SORN: A declaration that a vehicle is kept off public roads and is not taxed for road use.
Shared route: A path that pedestrians and cyclists may both use.
Sidelights: Low-power front and rear position lights; not bright enough alone for driving at speed.
Slippery road ahead: A warning that the road surface may be slippery.
Slippery road surface: A road that is wet, icy, or otherwise hard for tyres to grip.
Slippery road: A road surface with poor grip, so vehicles can skid more easily.
Snow plough: A vehicle that clears snow from the road, often with a blade at the front.
Speed camera: A camera that records vehicles breaking the speed limit.
Speed cameras: Cameras that detect vehicles exceeding the speed limit.
Speed humps: Raised sections across the road designed to slow traffic down.
Stabiliser: A device that reduces unwanted swinging or swaying of a trailer while towing.
Suspension: The springs and related parts that connect the wheels to the car body and absorb bumps.
T-junction: A junction where one road meets another and ends, forming a ‘T’ shape.
Temporary diversion: A short-term alternative route when the normal road cannot be used.
Temporary diversions: Short-term alternative routes when the normal road is closed or blocked.
Temporary lane closure: One or more lanes closed for a limited time, often during road works.
Temporary road works: Short-term construction or repairs that change normal road conditions.
Temporary traffic lights: Portable signals used for a limited time, often at road works.
Third party, fire and theft: Insurance that covers injury/damage to others, plus fire damage and theft of your vehicle.
Timing belt: A belt that keeps engine valves and pistons moving in the correct timing.
Tourist attractions: Places of interest for visitors, such as landmarks or museums.
Traffic calming: Road features designed to slow vehicles down, such as humps or narrowings.
Transmission: The system that transfers engine power to the wheels, including the gearbox.
Two-way traffic: Traffic moving in both directions on the same road.
Tyre grip: How well the tyres hold onto the road surface without sliding.
Tyres under-inflated: Tyres with too little air; can raise fuel use and affect braking.
U-turn: Turning the vehicle all the way round to go back the way you came.
U-turns: Turning the vehicle around in a U-shape to go back the way you came.
Uneven road surface: A bumpy or irregular road that can affect control and comfort.
Variable message signs: Electronic signs that change to show live warnings or instructions.
Vehicle registration document: The official paper (V5C / log book) that records who the vehicle is registered to.
Waiting restrictions: Rules that limit when you may wait or park along a stretch of road.
accelerator: The pedal that increases engine power and vehicle speed (also called the gas pedal).
adaptive cruise control: Cruise control that also adjusts speed to keep a gap from the vehicle ahead.
aggressive driving: Driving in a hostile or impatient way, such as tailgating or harsh speeding.
air brakes: A braking system on many large vehicles that uses compressed air instead of only hydraulic fluid.
airbag: A safety cushion that inflates quickly in a crash to protect occupants.
airway: The passage that lets air reach the lungs for breathing.
alertness: Being fully awake and ready to notice hazards and react quickly.
alternative route: A different path to the same destination if the usual road is blocked.
amber beacon: A flashing amber warning light, often used on slow or working vehicles.
amber flashing beacon: An orange warning light that flashes on a vehicle to make it more noticeable.
anti-dazzle: A rear-view mirror setting that reduces glare from headlights behind you at night.
approved driving course: A recognised training course (often for safer driving) that insurers may treat as a discount factor.
approved instructor: A driving teacher officially approved to give paid lessons (ADI in the UK).
aquaplaning: When tyres ride up on water and lose grip with the road surface.
arm signal: A hand signal given by the driver to show other road users what you intend to do.
authorised recycling site: An approved place that can safely take hazardous items like car batteries.
automatic transmission: A gearbox that changes gears for you, without a clutch pedal.
axles: The shafts that the wheels of a vehicle or trailer turn on.
barrier: A gate or arm that can block the road when a train is coming.
blind spots: Areas around the vehicle that you cannot see in your mirrors alone.
blind-spot assist: A system that warns if a vehicle is in an area you cannot see in your mirrors.
blind-spot monitoring: A system that warns you about vehicles in areas you cannot see in the mirrors.
blisters: Fluid-filled swellings on the skin that can form after burns; do not burst them.
blue flashing beacon: A flashing blue warning light used by certain emergency or specialist vehicles.
blue flashing lights: Emergency warning lights used by police, fire, ambulance, and similar services.
bodywork: The outer shell and panels of the vehicle (bonnet, wings, doors, etc.).
bollard: A short post on the road used to mark an island, edge, or obstruction.
box junction: A road junction painted with yellow criss-cross lines on the road surface.
brake lights: Red lights at the rear that come on when you press the brake pedal.
breakdown: When a vehicle stops working and can no longer be driven normally.
breaks down: Stops working so the vehicle cannot continue normally.
broken white lines: Dashed white road markings, often showing a boundary you may cross when safe.
built-up area: A town or village area with buildings beside the road; street lighting often marks a 30 mph zone.
built-up areas: Towns or villages with buildings close to the road; a 30 mph limit often applies with street lights.
bunching: When vehicles pack closely together, often causing sudden braking waves.
bus lane: A lane reserved for buses (and sometimes taxis/cycles) during the times shown on signs.
bus lanes: Lanes reserved mainly for buses (and sometimes taxis or cycles).
caravan: A trailer designed for living or camping, towed behind a vehicle.
carriageway: The part of the road used by vehicles, not the pavement or verge.
casualties: People injured in an accident or emergency.
casualty: An injured person in an accident.
central reservation: The strip or barrier that separates the two directions of traffic on a dual carriageway.
chest compressions: Repeated firm pushes on the centre of the chest during CPR to pump blood.
child restraint: A child seat or similar device that holds a child safely in the vehicle.
child seat: A special seat that holds a child safely with the correct restraints.
clearway: A road marked so that stopping on the main carriageway is tightly restricted.
clutch: The pedal that disconnects the engine from the wheels so you can change gear.
coasting downhill: Rolling down a slope without using the engine to help control speed.
coasting: Rolling along with the clutch pressed or in neutral, so the engine is not driving the wheels.
collision: A crash when vehicles or objects hit each other.
congestion: Heavy, slow-moving traffic when roads are overcrowded.
contradict: Say or show the opposite of something else.
contraflow system: A temporary traffic system where vehicles travel in the opposite direction to normal, often during roadworks.
contraflow: A temporary traffic system where vehicles travel in the opposite direction to normal, often during roadworks.
controlled parking zone: An area where parking is controlled by signs and marked bays at set times.
coolant: The liquid in the engine cooling system that helps stop the engine overheating.
countdown markers: Posts with decreasing bars (3, 2, 1) showing how close you are to a motorway exit.
country lane: A narrow rural road, often with limited space and visibility.
crawler or climbing lane: An extra uphill lane for slow vehicles so faster traffic is not held up.
crossroads: A junction where two roads cross, usually forming a plus-sign shape.
cruise control: A system that holds a set speed without keeping your foot on the accelerator.
cuts in: Moves suddenly into your lane or gap with little space in front of you.
cycle lane: A part of the road marked for cyclists, shown by a bicycle symbol and lane lines.
cyclist: A person riding a bicycle on the road.
dangerous goods: Hazardous materials (chemicals, fuels, etc.) needing special transport rules.
dashboard warning light: A light on the instrument panel that alerts you to a vehicle fault or important status.
dazzle: Temporarily blind someone with bright light.
dazzled: Temporarily blinded or unable to see clearly because of bright lights.
dazzling: Blinding other drivers with bright lights, such as brake lights in a queue at night.
debris: Scattered pieces of wreckage, objects, or rubbish left after a crash.
defibrillator (AED): A portable device that can deliver an electric shock to try to restart a heart in cardiac arrest.
demister: A control that clears mist from the windows so you can see clearly.
demisters: Controls that clear mist from the windows so you can see clearly.
diamond-shaped lane signs: White diamond road markings that show a lane reserved for particular vehicles.
diesel fuel cap: The cover that seals the diesel filler opening; if loose, fuel can spill onto the road.
dip your headlights: Switch from full beam to dipped (lower) beam so oncoming or overtaking drivers are not dazzled.
dipped headlights: Headlights aimed lower so they light the road without dazzling oncoming drivers.
dips: Low points in the road that can hide traffic until you are close.
disabled bays: Parking spaces reserved for vehicles displaying a valid Blue Badge.
dismounting: Getting off a bicycle (or motorcycle) to walk beside it.
diversion signs: Temporary signs that send traffic along a different route around a closure or roadworks.
door mirrors: The side mirrors mounted on the doors, used to see traffic beside and behind you.
double parked: Parked beside another parked vehicle, blocking a lane or space.
double yellow lines: Two yellow lines at the kerb meaning no waiting at any time (unless signs say otherwise).
drain covers: Metal lids over drains in the road surface; they can be slippery when wet.
drifting out of lane: Gradually moving sideways so the vehicle leaves its traffic lane.
drink- or drug-driving: Driving after drinking alcohol or taking drugs that impair your ability to drive.
driver drowsiness system: A driver-assistance feature that detects tired driving and alerts you.
driver-assistance system: Technology that helps the driver with safety, control, or alerts.
driveway: A private path from a house or property that joins the public road.
driving documents: Official papers such as your licence and insurance that prove you can drive legally.
drowsiness: Sleepiness that slows your thinking and reactions while driving.
drowsy: Feeling sleepy or half-asleep, so your reactions and attention are reduced.
dual carriageway: A major road with traffic travelling in opposite directions, separated by a central reservation.
dual carriageways: A major road with traffic travelling in opposite directions, separated by a central reservation.
dual controls: Extra pedals for the supervisor or instructor to help control the car.
dusk: The period of fading light after sunset when visibility drops.
edge forward: Move the car forward very slowly, a little at a time, to improve your view before joining the road.
embedded: Stuck inside the wound (for example glass or metal); do not pull it out yourself.
emerge: Come out onto the road from a side road, driveway, or similar entrance.
emergency area: A marked bay beside a motorway for stopping in an emergency when there is no hard shoulder.
emergency phone: A roadside phone on motorways for contacting emergency services if you break down.
emergency roadside telephone: A free phone fixed beside the motorway that links you to help and shows your location.
emergency services: Police, fire, and ambulance teams called to help at serious incidents.
emergency stop: Braking as quickly and safely as possible to avoid a collision.
emergency telephone: A free roadside phone on motorways that connects you to operators who can send help.
emerging: Coming out from a junction or side road onto another road.
engine braking: Slowing the vehicle by changing to a lower gear so the engine helps reduce speed.
engine revs: How fast the engine is turning; often shown on the rev counter (tachometer).
environmentally friendly: Causing less harm to the environment, e.g. lower emissions.
estate car: A car with an extended rear area for carrying more luggage.
exhaust emissions: Gases and particles released from a vehicle’s exhaust into the air.
farmland: Countryside used for farming, where animals or slow farm vehicles may be near the road.
fatigue: Extreme tiredness that reduces concentration and safe driving ability.
filler cap: The cover that seals the fuel tank opening after refuelling.
filtering: When motorcyclists or cyclists move carefully between lanes or past slow queues of traffic.
first aid kit: A set of basic medical supplies for treating minor injuries at the scene.
first aid: Immediate care given to an injured person before professional help arrives.
flash your headlights: Briefly switch headlights on and off only to let others know you are there—not to claim priority.
flashes headlights: Briefly switches headlights on and off—often to ask for room to pass, not to demand you speed up.
flashing amber lights: Orange warning lights that flash to alert drivers, often near schools when children may be about.
flashing amber: An amber traffic light that blinks on and off at a pelican crossing.
flood water: Water covering part of the road after heavy rain or flooding, which can wet the brakes.
floodwater: Deep water covering the road after heavy rain or flooding.
fog lights: Extra lights for very poor visibility in fog; use only when conditions are bad enough.
following distance: The gap you leave between your vehicle and the one in front.
following very closely: Driving with too little space behind another vehicle (tailgating), which is unsafe.
footbrake: The main brake pedal operated with your foot to slow or stop the vehicle.
footpaths: Paths for people walking, usually beside a road (pavements/sidewalks).
four-wheel drive: A system that sends power to all four wheels to improve grip, especially on slippery or uneven surfaces.
front fog lights: Extra front lights used only when visibility is seriously reduced, such as in thick fog.
fuel consumption: How much fuel the vehicle uses; higher use means more cost and emissions.
fuel-efficient driving: Driving in a way that uses less fuel, often by smoother acceleration and steadier speed.
full beam headlights: Headlights on their brightest setting; can dazzle others if used wrongly.
full beam: Headlights on their brightest, longest setting; can dazzle others, so not for use in fog or when meeting traffic.
full-beam headlights: Headlights on their brightest, longest setting; must be dipped so you do not dazzle other drivers.
give way: Let other traffic go first when they have priority, instead of continuing ahead of them.
give-way lines: Road markings at a junction where you must let other traffic go first.
goods vehicles: Vehicles built mainly to carry cargo rather than passengers.
green flashing beacon: A flashing green warning light used by certain medical vehicles responding to emergencies.
green plates: Optional green ‘P’ plates some new drivers display to show they are newly qualified.
hand-held mobile phone: A mobile phone that you hold in your hand while using it.
handbook: The vehicle’s owner manual with operating and safety information.
handbrake: The parking brake, normally used to hold the vehicle when stopped, not for slowing in motion.
hands-free phone: A phone you can use without holding it, for example with a speaker or Bluetooth kit.
hard shoulder: The emergency lane at the side of a motorway, normally for stopping only in an emergency.
harsh braking: Braking suddenly and hard instead of smoothly and early.
hatched area: A painted zone with diagonal stripes that separates traffic streams.
hazard lights: All indicators flashing together to warn others of a hazard or breakdown.
hazard markings: Warning symbols or plates that show a load’s danger type.
hazard warning lights: Both indicators flashing together to warn other drivers of a hazard or sudden slowing.
hazard warning sign: A triangular road sign that warns of a danger or difficult situation ahead on the road.
hazard: Anything on or near the road that could cause danger or force you to change speed or direction.
hazards: Short for hazard warning lights: all indicators flashing to warn of danger or a stop.
head restraint: The padded support behind your head on the seat, often called a headrest.
heavy bleeding: A lot of blood loss from a wound that needs urgent pressure and help.
heavy spray: Water thrown up by tyres on a wet road, which can reduce visibility.
herding animals: Moving livestock (such as sheep or cattle) along or across a road.
hi-vis: High-visibility clothing (bright/reflective) that makes a person easier to see, especially in poor light.
high street: The main shopping street in a town or city centre.
high-sided vehicle: A tall vehicle such as a lorry or van that can be strongly affected by side winds.
hill crest: The top of a hill where your view of the road ahead is often limited.
horse rider: A person riding a horse on or beside the road; treat them as vulnerable road users.
horse riders: People riding horses on or beside the road.
humpback bridge: A bridge with a sharp rise in the middle that can hide traffic beyond it.
incident: An accident, breakdown, or other unexpected event on the road.
indicating: Using your direction indicators to show you intend to turn or change lane.
indicators: Flashing lights on a vehicle used to show you intend to turn or change lane.
insurance certificate: A document that proves your vehicle has valid insurance cover.
insurance: A policy that can cover costs after an accident, damage, or claim.
interior mirror: The rear-view mirror inside the car, usually at the top of the windscreen.
junction: A place where roads meet or cross, such as a T-junction or crossroads.
junctions: Places where roads meet or cross; smaller road users can be harder to spot there.
kerb: The raised stone or concrete edge between the road and the pavement (US: curb).
kick-down: Pressing the accelerator hard in an automatic car so it changes to a lower gear for quicker acceleration.
lane closures: When one or more lanes are temporarily closed, often due to roadworks or an incident.
lane markings: Painted lines on the road that show where each traffic lane is.
large goods vehicles: Big trucks that carry freight; often called LGVs in the UK.
leaded fuel: Older petrol that contained lead; not used for normal road cars today.
learner driver: Someone learning to drive, often showing L plates on the vehicle.
left lane: In the UK, the lane nearest the left-hand side of the road (kerb side) for normal driving.
level crossing: A place where a road crosses a railway line, often with barriers and warning lights.
level crossings: A place where a road crosses a railway line, often with barriers and warning lights.
licensing authority (DVLA): The official body that issues and manages driving licences (Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency).
licensing authority: The official body that issues and manages driving licences (in Great Britain, the DVLA).
limited visibility: When you cannot see far enough ahead because something blocks your view.
live lane: A lane that is open for normal moving traffic (not closed or for emergency use only).
livestock: Farm animals such as sheep or cattle that may be on or near the road.
long vehicle: A very lengthy type of road vehicle, such as a lorry, coach, or articulated truck.
loose chippings: Small loose stones on a newly surfaced road that can fly up and damage vehicles.
loose gravel: Small stones on the road surface that can make tyres slip more easily.
lorries: Large goods vehicles used to carry freight (UK term for trucks).
lorry: A large goods vehicle used for carrying cargo (also called a truck).
low-flying aircraft: Planes flying near the ground, often near an airport approach.
lower gears: Gears with more engine power and less speed, useful on hills.
main beam: High-beam headlights that light farther ahead but can dazzle other road users.
main road: A larger, busier road that smaller side roads join onto.
main-beam headlights: The high-intensity headlight setting (full beam) for dark roads with no oncoming traffic.
major road: The more important road at a junction, which usually has priority.
mandatory instruction: An order you must follow, not just advice.
mandatory route: A route you are required to follow, not just a suggested direction.
mandatory speed limit: A speed limit you must obey by law, often shown in a red circle or on overhead gantry signs.
manoeuvre: A controlled driving movement such as reversing, turning, or parking.
marker posts: Small roadside posts that show distance markers and the direction to the nearest emergency phone.
maximum authorised mass: The heaviest legal weight of a vehicle or trailer including its load (also called MAM).
medically exempt: Excused from a legal requirement for approved medical reasons.
metres: A metric unit of length used on UK height and width restriction signs.
mileage marker: A roadside post or sign showing distance along a route, often in miles.
mini-roundabout: A small roundabout, often marked by a white painted circle on the road.
moped: A small, low-powered motorcycle that often travels more slowly than cars.
mopeds: Low-powered two-wheel motor vehicles, lighter and slower than most motorcycles.
motor insurance: Legal cover for using a motor vehicle on public roads, protecting against claims from others at minimum.
motor vehicles: Powered road vehicles such as cars, vans, and motorcycles (not bicycles or pedestrians).
motorcycle restriction: A rule that limits or bans motorcycles on that stretch of road.
motorcyclist: A person riding a motorcycle; they can be less stable and harder to see than cars.
motorcyclists: People riding motorcycles; they can be hidden in blind spots and move up beside you quickly.
motorway services: Rest areas on a motorway with fuel, food, and toilets.
motorway: A high-speed dual-direction road with controlled access for most traffic, shown by blue signs in the UK.
motorways: High-speed roads with controlled access for most traffic, shown by blue signs in the UK.
move off: To start moving from a stopped position, such as pulling away from the kerb or after waiting.
moving off: Starting to drive away after you have been stationary.
narrow bridge: A bridge where the road is too narrow for two vehicles to pass easily side by side.
narrowing: The road becoming less wide ahead.
national speed limit: The default UK speed limit when no numbered limit signs are shown (varies by road type and vehicle).
neck injuries: Damage to the neck bones, muscles, or spinal cord that can be serious after a crash.
neutral: A gear position where the engine is not connected to the wheels.
nose weight: The downward weight a trailer’s hitch puts on the vehicle’s tow ball; it must stay within limits.
number plate: The plate on a vehicle that shows its registration number.
obscured: Partly hidden or hard to see, for example by dirt, trees, or another object.
obstruction: Something blocking the road so traffic cannot pass freely.
obstructs: Blocks or gets in the way of other traffic so it cannot pass freely.
octagonal: Eight-sided shape; in the UK the STOP sign is octagonal.
oncoming traffic: Vehicles travelling toward you from the opposite direction.
one-way road: A road where traffic is allowed to travel in only one direction.
one-way street: A street where traffic is allowed to travel in only one direction.
one-way streets: A street where traffic is allowed to travel in only one direction.
overhead lane signals: Lights above each lane that show whether that lane is open or closed to traffic.
overloaded: Carrying more weight than the vehicle or trailer is legally allowed to carry.
overtake a horse and rider: Pass a person riding a horse on the road; horses can be startled by noise and speed.
overtake: To pass a slower vehicle ahead by moving past it into another lane.
overtaken: When another vehicle has passed you and moved ahead of you.
overtaking traffic: Vehicles that are passing you or about to pass you.
overtaking: Passing a slower vehicle by moving alongside and ahead of it.
parking brake: The brake (often a handbrake) that holds the vehicle still when parked.
parking lights: Dim sidelights left on when parked so others can see your vehicle at night.
parking restrictions: Rules that limit where and when you may park, shown by signs or road markings.
passing place: A widened section of a narrow road where vehicles can pass or wait.
passing places: Widened spots on a narrow road where vehicles can pull in to let others pass.
pavement: The raised path beside the road for people walking (sidewalk).
peak traffic hours: The busiest times of day when roads are most congested (rush hour).
peak traffic times: Busy periods when many people travel, often morning and evening rush hours.
pedestrian crossing: A marked place on the road where people on foot can cross safely.
pedestrian-only zones: Areas where motor vehicles are normally not allowed and only people on foot may use the space.
pelican crossing: A pedestrian crossing controlled by traffic lights, including a flashing amber phase.
penalty points: Points added to your driving licence after certain traffic offences.
powered mobility scooters: Small electric vehicles for people with limited mobility, usually for pavements and short trips.
primary route: A major UK road between towns and cities, usually signed in green with white lettering.
priority: The right to go first when roads meet or when rules give you precedence.
prohibition: A rule that forbids a particular action or type of vehicle.
provisional licence: A learner driving licence that allows practice driving under set restrictions before a full licence.
pull away: When a vehicle starts moving off from a stop, such as leaving a bus stop.
pull over: Move to the side of the road and stop safely.
pulls to one side: The vehicle steers or veers left or right by itself when you brake or drive.
puncture: A flat tyre caused by a hole that lets the air out.
push-button signals: Pedestrian traffic lights started by pressing a button at the crossing.
queue: A line of vehicles waiting or moving slowly.
queues: Lines of slow-moving or waiting traffic.
railway crossing: A place where a road crosses railway tracks, often with lights, barriers, or alarms.
rear fog lights: Bright red lights at the back of a vehicle used only in thick fog to help others see you.
rear-facing baby seat: A child seat that faces backwards, safer for infants in a crash.
recovery position: A side-lying first-aid position that helps keep an unconscious breathing person’s airway clear.
red route: A road marked with red lines where stopping and parking are tightly controlled.
red routes: UK roads marked with red lines where stopping and parking are tightly restricted.
reflective clothing: Clothes that shine when light hits them, helping others see the wearer.
reflective safety markers: Bright reflective strips or panels that help others see a vehicle, especially in the dark.
reflective studs: Cat’s-eye markers set in the road that reflect light to show lane edges at night.
reflective yellow school warning sign: A bright yellow sign that warns drivers they are near a school.
refuge area: A safe lay-by beside a motorway where you can stop if you have a problem.
registered keeper: The person named on the vehicle registration as responsible for the vehicle records.
registration document: The V5C paper that records the vehicle’s details and its registered keeper.
residential area: A neighbourhood of homes where traffic and pedestrians are often close together.
residential streets: Roads in housing areas where people live, often with parked cars and pedestrians.
restraint: A safety device that holds a child securely in the vehicle, such as a child seat.
restraints: Straps, ropes, or other fittings used to hold a load firmly in place.
restriction: A limit on what you may do, such as speed, access, or vehicle type.
right of way: Who is allowed to go first when paths cross or meet.
right-hand bend: A curve in the road that turns to the right as you travel along it.
right-hand lane: On a UK multi-lane motorway, the lane furthest to the right, normally for overtaking.
road camber: The slight slope built across the road surface, usually higher in the middle.
road humps: Raised bumps in the road surface used to slow traffic.
road markings: Lines, symbols, or writing painted on the road surface to guide or control traffic.
road narrowing: The road becoming less wide, so careful positioning is needed.
road narrows: The carriageway becomes narrower ahead, so there is less space for vehicles.
road surface: The top layer of the road that tyres touch (e.g. tarmac, snow, ice, or loose gravel).
road works: Construction or repairs on the road that may change lanes or reduce speed.
roadworks: Road repairs or building work that may close paths or change traffic.
roof rack: A frame fitted on a vehicle’s roof for carrying extra loads.
roundabout: A circular junction where traffic usually travels clockwise and you give way to traffic already on it.
route numbers: Official road identifiers such as A1 or M25 shown on direction signs.
route planner: A map or app that suggests roads and directions for a journey.
safe gap: The clear space you keep ahead of your vehicle so you can stop safely if traffic slows or stops.
sat nav: Satellite navigation: a GPS device or app that gives driving directions.
school crossing patrol: A trained person (often called a lollipop person) who helps children cross safely near schools.
school crossing: A place near a school where children cross the road, often with special signs or a crossing patrol.
school warning sign: A triangular sign showing children, warning that a school is nearby and extra care is needed.
scrapped: When a vehicle is officially destroyed or broken up and removed from the road fleet.
secondary coupling device: A backup link (often a chain or cable) that keeps the trailer attached if the main coupling fails.
security-coded radio: A car radio that needs a code after power loss, making it useless to thieves.
service area: A motorway services site with parking, fuel, and facilities where you can stop safely to rest.
service schedule: The maker’s planned times for checks, oil changes, and maintenance.
severe burns: Serious burn injuries that need careful cooling and urgent medical help.
sharp bend: A curve in the road that turns tightly and may need a clear speed reduction.
shock: A serious medical condition after injury when the body is not circulating blood well.
shoulder check: Looking over your shoulder to see areas the mirrors may miss.
side road: A smaller road that joins a main road.
side winds: Strong wind blowing across the road from the side, which can push a vehicle off its line.
sidecar: A one-wheeled passenger compartment fixed to the side of a motorcycle.
sidelights: Small, low-power lights used to make a parked or moving vehicle more visible.
sidewall cuts: Cuts or damage in the side wall of a tyre that can make it illegal or unsafe.
signal operator: The person who controls railway signals and barriers at a level crossing.
signalling: Using indicators (or other signals) to show other road users what you intend to do.
single carriageway: A road without a central reservation separating opposite directions of traffic.
single carriageways: A road without a central reservation separating opposite directions of traffic.
single-track road: A narrow road wide enough for only one vehicle, so drivers may need to wait to pass.
skid marks: Marks left on the road when tyres lose grip; on warning signs they often mean a slippery road ahead.
skidding: When tyres lose grip and the vehicle slides instead of staying under control.
slip road: The short linking road used to join or leave a motorway.
slippery road: A road surface with poor tyre grip, so vehicles can skid more easily.
snow chains: Metal chains fitted around tyres to improve grip in deep snow or ice.
solid white line: An unbroken white road marking that often means you must not cross or enter.
sounding of horns: Using the vehicle horn to make a warning sound.
speed camera zone: An area where cameras check vehicle speeds for enforcement.
speed hump: A raised ridge across the road that forces drivers to slow down.
speed humps: Raised ridges across the road that force drivers to slow down (also called sleeping policemen).
speed limiters: Devices that restrict how fast a large vehicle can go, often required by law for lorries.
spray: Water thrown up by tyres on a wet road that reduces how far you can see.
stabiliser: A device that helps reduce swaying of a trailer or caravan while towing.
staggered junction: A junction where side roads join from left and right at slightly different points, not opposite each other.
stalls: The engine stops unexpectedly, often when starting or changing gear.
stationary traffic: Vehicles that have stopped and are not moving, often in a queue.
stationary: Not moving; the vehicle is at a complete stop.
steep downhill: A sharp slope going downwards where speed can increase quickly.
steep upward slope: A sharp uphill climb where the road rises quickly.
steering lock: A security lock that stops the steering wheel turning when the key is removed.
steering vibration: Shaking felt through the steering wheel while driving.
stop line: The solid white line at a junction that marks where you must stop when required.
stopping distance: The total distance needed to stop: thinking distance plus braking distance.
stopping time: How long you have to react and brake before you would hit the vehicle ahead.
straddle: Drive with wheels on both sides of a line, partly crossing it.
studs: Raised reflective road markers that help show where lanes and edges are, especially at night.
supplementary plates: Small rectangular signs placed under a main road sign that add details such as times or exceptions.
sway: Side-to-side swinging of a trailer or caravan while being towed, which can become dangerous.
swerve: A sudden change of direction to avoid something, such as a pothole or slippery patch.
swerving: Suddenly changing direction, often to avoid something in the road.
swings right: Moves out to the right before turning left—common for long vehicles that need more space.
tail lights: The red lights at the rear of a vehicle that show its position to drivers behind.
taxing the vehicle: Paying UK vehicle tax (VED) so the vehicle can be used on public roads.
temporary obstruction: Something briefly blocking or slowing traffic, such as a stopped vehicle.
temporary speed limit: A speed limit that applies only for a limited time, often near roadworks.
three-lane motorway: A motorway with three lanes in each direction of travel.
tinted lenses: Lenses that are darkened or coloured, reducing how much light reaches your eyes.
tonnes: A metric unit of weight used on UK restriction signs for heavy vehicles.
tow ball: The ball-shaped coupling on a tow bar that the trailer hitch locks onto.
tow bar: The metal bar fitted to a vehicle for attaching and towing a trailer or caravan.
towed caravan: A caravan being pulled behind another vehicle on the road.
towing a trailer: Pulling a trailer attached behind your vehicle.
towing: Pulling a trailer, caravan, or another vehicle behind your car using a tow bar or hitch.
tractor: A slow agricultural vehicle often seen on country roads; overtaking needs clear space and time.
traffic officer: An official authorised to manage traffic on motorways and some major roads.
traffic officers: Specialist road staff who manage incidents and traffic on motorways and major A-roads.
traffic-calming measures: Road features such as humps or narrowings designed to keep vehicle speeds lower.
trailer: An unpowered wheeled unit designed to be towed behind a vehicle to carry loads.
trams: Electric passenger vehicles that run on rails set into the road surface.
transverse lines: Lines painted across the road (often yellow) to alert you as you approach a hazard.
transverse yellow road markings: Yellow lines painted across the road (from side to side), not along it.
tread depth: How deep the grooves in a tyre are; worn-down tread reduces grip, especially in wet weather.
triangular warning sign: A red-bordered triangle road sign that warns of a hazard ahead.
tunnel: A road passage that goes under ground or through a hill.
two-second following gap: A rule of thumb: stay at least two seconds behind the vehicle ahead in good, dry conditions.
two-second following rule: In good, dry conditions, keep at least a two-second gap behind the vehicle ahead.
two-way road: A road where traffic travels in both directions.
two-way roads: Roads where traffic travels in both directions.
tyre grip: How well the tyres hold the road surface for steering and braking.
tyre pressure: How much air is in each tyre; incorrect pressure affects handling, braking, and tyre wear.
tyre pressures: How much air is in each tyre; incorrect pressure affects handling, braking, and tyre wear.
tyre wear: How the tyre rubber wears down; uneven wear can signal a fault.
unattended: Left alone with no one in or watching the vehicle.
unbraked trailer: A trailer without its own brakes; coupling safety devices are especially important.
unconscious: Not awake and not responding; may need emergency help.
under-inflated tyres: Tyres with too little air pressure, which can worsen handling and wear.
uneven road surface: A road that is bumpy or irregular rather than smooth.
unlit road: A road with no street lighting at night.
unmarked crossroads: A junction where roads meet with no give-way or stop signs or road markings.
uphill climb: A section of road going up a slope.
urban clearway: An urban road where stopping is restricted during posted times, except briefly for passengers.
urban pollution: Air and noise pollution in towns and cities, often from traffic.
variable speed limits: Temporary speed limits shown on overhead signs that change with traffic conditions.
vehicle ownership: Who legally owns the vehicle; changes of ownership must be recorded with the DVLA.
vehicle registration certificate: Another name for the V5C registration document showing vehicle and keeper details.
vehicle registration document: The V5C paper that records the vehicle’s details and its registered keeper.
vehicle registration: The official number plate details that identify a vehicle.
vehicle tax: The UK road tax (VED) you must pay to use a vehicle on public roads.
verge: The soft or grassy edge beside the road, not meant for normal driving.
visibility is seriously reduced: UK phrase meaning you can see only a short distance, often under about 100 metres.
vulnerable: More at risk of injury in a collision because of little physical protection (e.g. bikes, motorcycles, pedestrians).
warden: A parking or traffic warden who enforces parking rules.
warning triangle: A red reflective triangle placed on the road to warn others of a broken-down vehicle.
water pooling: Water collecting in low spots on the road after rain.
wheelspin: When drive wheels spin too fast on a slippery surface and lose grip.
winding road: A road with many bends, where overtaking is often difficult and slow traffic can build up.
windscreen pillars: The upright frames at the edges of the windscreen that can block part of your view.
windsock: A cone-shaped cloth tube that shows wind direction and strength; used as a road-sign symbol.
yellow lines: Yellow road markings at the kerb that restrict waiting or parking.
zebra crossing: A pedestrian crossing with black-and-white stripes where drivers must give way to people waiting to cross.
zebra crossings: A pedestrian crossing with black-and-white stripes where drivers must give way to people waiting to cross.
zig-zag road markings: Yellow zig-zag lines near crossings or schools where you must not park or stop and block the view.
zigzag lines: Zigzag road markings near crossings; parking and waiting there is restricted.
